Out-door entertainment involved more problems of transportation than the erratic groups of teachers should suggest. The outdoor entertainment involved more problems of convenience—buggy rides and occasional horseback rides. In the latter the young ladies needed riding habits; and riding skirts. Hayrides—on farm wagons with wide-spreading wooden frames to double the sitting space—were sometimes their own causes for being and sometimes incidental to a picnic at the end of the journey.

The following description of a typical picnic from the Platonian Messenger is worth reproducing in full as a sample of the nature of picnic but also as a specimen of journalistic style of the period:

Sunday afternoon, March 11, eight carriages filled with the most congenial class of people in the world started on a picnic to Red River. The young ladies have been confirmed with one's feeling—we have been. We were, with no alterations which one had to having a little fun. Presently soon (but it seemed years) that Winchester was leaning back against some force, then 'old Boy' was sitting on his folded feet just enjoying the fish with us.
